catalog_quote: Mateo Toledo (2017) muestra que las palabras en final de frase o aisladas llevan acento en la última sílaba; en cambio, en posición no final lo llevan en la primera. La frase prosódica en (9a), que contiene varias palabras fonológicas, ilustra el patrón de acento que sólo se observa en las bisilábicas chib’ej y komana’ —las monosilábicas llevan acento en su única sílaba—. La palabra chib’ej lleva acento en la primera sílaba porque ocurre en medio de la frase y komana’, en la última sílaba porque ocurre al final. ... El patrón anterior es resultado de la interacción entre la prominencia de la palabra y la prominencia frasal; la de la palabra recae sobre la primera sílaba, como en chib’ej en (9a), a lo cual llamamos ‘acento de palabra’; en cambio, la de tipo frasal, que llamamos ‘acento frasal’, ocurre al final de la frase y se ancla a la última sílaba de la última palabra, como en komana…

new_statements.quote: Mateo Toledo (2017) muestra que las palabras en final de frase o aisladas llevan acento en la última sílaba; en cambio, en posición no final lo llevan en la primera. [...] la de la palabra recae sobre la primera sílaba, como en chib’ej en (9a), a lo cual llamamos ‘acento de palabra’; en cambio, la de tipo frasal, que llamamos ‘acento frasal’, ocurre al final de la frase y se ancla a la última sílaba de la última palabra [...] este último predomina porque una palabra en final de frase sólo lleva acento frasal. [...] Finalmente, las palabras aisladas en (9b) se tratan como frases y, por ello, se acentúan en la última sílaba (nunca en la primera).
new_statements.translation: Mateo Toledo (2017) shows that phrase-final or isolated words carry stress on the last syllable; in non-final position, by contrast, they carry it on the first. [...] word prominence falls on the first syllable, as in chib'ej in (9a), which we call 'word stress'; phrasal prominence, which we call 'phrasal accent', occurs at the end of the phrase and is anchored to the last syllable of the last word [...] the latter prevails because a phrase-final word carries only phrasal accent. [...] Finally, the isolated words in (9b) are treated as phrases and therefore are stressed on the last syllable (never on the first).

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (46 pp., text layer, Signos Lingüísticos 13(25), 2017, pp. 8-53). Section 4 'El acento en la palabra y frase' begins on printed p. 19 = PDF p. 12 and runs to p. 20 = PDF p. 13; Table 1 (duration/intensity/pitch of /i, e/ in chib'ej phrase-medial vs phrase-final) is on printed p. 21 = PDF p. 14. Every segment of the quote is present verbatim at that locator: 'Mateo Toledo (2017) muestra que las palabras en final de frase o aisladas llevan acento en la última sílaba; en cambio, en posición no final lo llevan en la primera' (p. 19); 'la de la palabra recae sobre la primera sílaba, como en chib'ej en (9a), a lo cual llamamos 'acento de palabra'; en cambio, la de tipo frasal, que llamamos…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word-level stress is on the first syllable of the phonological word; a phrase-level accent falls on the last syllable of the last word of the prosodic phrase and overrides word stress there. Because an isolated word is itself a phrase, citation forms surface with final stress (this is what Lichtman et al. 2010 and the ALMG 2005 grammar report as 'final stress'). Monosyllables are stressed on their only syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described as such in the 2017 paper. Lichtman et al. 2010 (p. 16) speculate that syllables with ejective consonants may receive secondary stress in connected speech and note that Barreno et al. 2005 find the accent 'somewhat flexible'.
new_statements.exceptions: Set A (ergative/possessive) prefixes can be extrametrical: they do not count for stress when they form a syllable separate from the root (ha- in hawajb'aj) but do when syllabified with it (j- in jixim) (fn. 6, p. 20, citing Kaufman 2015 and Mateo Toledo 2017). Lichtman et al. 2010: Spanish loans such as norte appeared with both syllables stressed. Stress is not contrastive (Lichtman et al. 2010, fn. 3).
new_statements.domain_note: Two domains explicitly distinguished: 'acento de palabra' (phonological word, initial syllable, incl. clitics/particles that can form a phonological word) vs 'acento frasal' (prosodic phrase, final syllable). Citation forms/words in isolation = final. Data from Santa Eulalia (Jolom Konob'). Bennett 2016 (p. 496) warns such phrasally conditioned shifts may reflect intonational contours rather than word stress; an alternative catalog reading is fixed: final syllable (isolation forms).
new_statements.identity_note: All first-hand sources describe the Santa Eulalia (Jolom Konob') variety of Q'anjob'al proper (qanj1241); Santa Eulalia is described as linguistically conservative (Lichtman et al. 2010 citing Raymundo et al. 2005). Zavala 1992 'El kanjobal de San Miguel Acatán', which surfaces in searches, is Akatek (acat1239), not this language.

sources.note: Sec. 4 'El acento en la palabra y frase' (pp. 19-20): phrase-final and isolated words stressed on the last syllable; non-final (phrase-medial) words on the first syllable; authors call the initial-syllable prominence 'acento de palabra' and the final one 'acento frasal' (anchored to the last syllable of the last word of the prosodic phrase); phrasal accent wins at phrase end; isolated words are treated as phrases; Set A prefixes can be extrametrical (fn. 6); acoustic table p. 21 shows duration/pitch correlates. Santa Eulalia data.

sources.note: fn. 3 p. 2: 'Stress falls on the last syllable of words in isolation, and also tends to fall on the last syllable of phrases.. it is not contrastive.' Sec. 4 Suprasegmentals p. 16: no lexical tone; in single-word elicitation stress always on the final syllable, 'in agreement with Barreno et al. (2005: 57)'; Spanish loans like norte had both syllables stressed; in the North Wind text non-final syllables appeared stressed (e.g. /ˈɛktoχ/, /ˈq'otbil/), possibly secondary stress on ejective syllables; Barreno et al. 2005 find the accent 'somewhat flexible'. One Santa Eulalia speaker.
